blocks.title: Pathogens and first defences
blocks.md: A **pathogen** is an organism or virus that causes disease. Types: **bacteria** (e.g. *Vibrio cholerae*), **viruses** (HIV), **fungi** (ringworm) and **protoctists** (*Plasmodium*). Non-specific defences: **skin**, **mucus and cilia**, stomach acid, lysozyme in tears, and **phagocytes**, which engulf pathogens (phagocytosis) and digest them with lysosomal enzymes. **Inflammation** and fever help too.

blocks.title: Antigen and antibody
blocks.md: An **antigen** is a molecule (often on the surface of a pathogen) that triggers an immune response; an **antibody** is a protein made in response that binds to one specific antigen. Antibodies are **specific**: their variable regions have a shape complementary to one antigen. Do not say the body makes antibodies 'to kill' directly; they label, agglutinate and neutralise, and phagocytes then destroy the pathogen.

items.text: Antigen of a pathogen is detected
Matching B cell is selected and divides
Memory cells remain in the blood

blocks.title: Specific response
blocks.md:
- **B cells**: recognise a specific antigen, divide (clonal selection) into **plasma cells** (secrete antibodies) and **memory cells**.
- **T helper cells** release cytokines that stimulate B cells and others.
- **T killer cells** attack infected body cells.
The response to the first infection (**primary**) is slow; on re-infection, memory cells give a faster, larger **secondary** response.

blocks.title: Antibody structure
blocks.md: An antibody (immunoglobulin) has **four polypeptide chains**, two heavy and two light, joined by disulfide bonds. The **variable region** at the tips forms the antigen-binding site, so different antibodies fit different antigens. The **constant region** is the same for each class. Antibodies bind to pathogens and cause them to clump (agglutination), neutralise toxins and make phagocytosis easier.

blocks.title: Worked example — doubling
blocks.statement: A B cell with the correct receptor divides every 8 hours. Starting from 1 selected cell, how many cells are there after 48 hours?

blocks.title: Worked example — primary and secondary
blocks.statement: After a first exposure to an antigen antibody concentration peaks at 10 units after 14 days. After a second exposure it peaks at 100 units after 5 days. Explain the difference.
steps: The first exposure needs selection of rare B cells and clone formation (slow).
Memory cells from the first exposure respond quickly in the second.
So more plasma cells form sooner and the peak is higher (secondary response).
blocks.answer: Memory cells give a faster, bigger response

blocks.title: Four infectious diseases
blocks.md:
- **Cholera**: *Vibrio cholerae* (bacterium); spread by contaminated water and food; severe diarrhoea.
- **Malaria**: *Plasmodium* (protoctist); spread by the female *Anopheles* mosquito (the **vector**).
- **Tuberculosis**: *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*; spread by droplets from coughs; affects the lungs.
- **HIV/AIDS**: a retrovirus infecting helper T cells; spread by body fluids; the immune system is weakened over time.

blocks.title: Active versus passive
blocks.md: In **active** immunity the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (after infection or vaccination): slow to start but long-lasting. In **passive** immunity antibodies are received ready-made (across the placenta, in breast milk or by injection): fast but short-lived and no memory cells. **Natural** = through infection or mother; **artificial** = through vaccination or injected antibodies. A vaccine does not cure; it prepares the body.

blocks.caption: Illustration of 75 % of a population being immune (herd immunity threshold for R₀ = 4).
blocks.alt: A bar chart with two bars: 25 percent not immune and 75 percent immune.

blocks.title: Vaccination and herd immunity
blocks.md: A **vaccine** contains weakened, killed or part of a pathogen (antigens), so that the body makes memory cells. **Herd immunity** is the protection of non-immune people when a high proportion of the population is immune. If R₀ is the average number of people one case infects in a fully susceptible population, the threshold is about 1 − 1 ÷ R₀.

blocks.title: Prevention and control
blocks.md: Control measures include safe drinking water and sanitation (cholera), bed nets, drainage of standing water and prompt treatment (malaria), vaccination programmes, early diagnosis and full courses of antibiotics (TB). **Antibiotic resistance** arises when mutated bacteria survive and multiply, so antibiotics must be used only when necessary. Health advice in this lesson must be checked by a health professional.

blocks.title: Worked example — herd immunity
blocks.statement: Suppose a disease has R₀ = 4. Estimate the proportion of the population that must be immune to stop sustained spread.

blocks.title: Worked example — classify immunity
blocks.statement: A newborn baby in Bafoussam receives antibodies from the mother's milk. Classify this immunity.
steps: The baby did not make the antibodies: passive.
They came naturally, not by injection: natural.
No memory cells are made, so protection is temporary.
